claim: The MHC region is highly associated with autoimmune and infectious diseases.
source: The MHC region is highly associated with autoimmune and infectious diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about the MHC region.

claim: The study used WGS from 419 individuals to call eight-digit HLA types.
source: Here we conduct an in-depth interrogation of associations between genetic variation, gene expression and disease. We create a comprehensive map of regulatory variation in the MHC region using WGS from 419 individuals to call eight-digit HLA types and RNA-seq data from matched iPSCs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of individuals and the resolution of HLA typing performed.

claim: The study used RNA-seq data from matched iPSCs.
source: We create a comprehensive map of regulatory variation in the MHC region using WGS from 419 individuals to call eight-digit HLA types and RNA-seq data from matched iPSCs.
evidence: The abstract states that RNA-seq data from iPSCs was used in the study.

claim: The study explored GWAS signals for 4083 traits.
source: Building on this regulatory map, we explored GWAS signals for 4083 traits, detecting colocalization for 180 disease loci with eQTLs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of traits examined.

claim: Colocalization was detected for 180 disease loci with eQTLs.
source: Building on this regulatory map, we explored GWAS signals for 4083 traits, detecting colocalization for 180 disease loci with eQTLs.
evidence: The abstract reports the number of disease loci showing colocalization.

claim: eQTL analyses taking HLA type haplotypes into account have substantially greater power compared with only using single variants.
source: We show that eQTL analyses taking HLA type haplotypes into account have substantially greater power compared with only using single variants.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding about the comparative power of different eQTL analysis approaches.

claim: The 8.1 ancestral haplotype is associated with delayed colonization in Cystic Fibrosis.
source: We examined the association between the 8.1 ancestral haplotype and delayed colonization in Cystic Fibrosis, postulating that downregulation of RNF5 expression is the likely causal mechanism.
evidence: The abstract states this association was examined in the study.

claim: Downregulation of RNF5 expression is the likely causal mechanism underlying the association between 8.1AH and delayed colonization in CF patients.
source: We examined the association between the 8.1 ancestral haplotype and delayed colonization in Cystic Fibrosis, postulating that downregulation of RNF5 expression is the likely causal mechanism.
evidence: The abstract explicitly postulates this mechanism based on the study findings.

claim: The MHC region is 4 Mb in size and located on chromosome 6p21.3.
source: The 4 Mb major histocompatibility (MHC) region on chromosome 6p21.3, which encodes the human leucocyte antigen (HLA) gene complex, is highly polymorphic, gene dense, and has strong linkage disequilibrium (LD) (Dendrou et al., 2018; Fehrmann et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction provides the size and chromosomal location of the MHC region with citations.

claim: The MHC region is highly polymorphic, gene dense, and has strong linkage disequilibrium.
source: The 4 Mb major histocompatibility (MHC) region on chromosome 6p21.3, which encodes the human leucocyte antigen (HLA) gene complex, is highly polymorphic, gene dense, and has strong linkage disequilibrium (LD) (Dendrou et al., 2018; Fehrmann et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction describes these characteristics of the MHC region with supporting citations.

claim: GWAS have identified many autoimmune and infectious diseases that are more prevalent in individuals carrying certain HLA types.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many autoimmune and infectious diseases that are more prevalent in individuals carrying certain HLA types (alleles), whereas other HLA types are protective against disease (Blackwell et al., 2009; Gough and Simmonds, 2007; Matzaraki et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction states this finding from previous GWAS with supporting citations.

claim: Some HLA types are protective against disease.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many autoimmune and infectious diseases that are more prevalent in individuals carrying certain HLA types (alleles), whereas other HLA types are protective against disease (Blackwell et al., 2009; Gough and Simmonds, 2007; Matzaraki et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction states that some HLA types have protective effects with supporting citations.

claim: The molecular mechanisms by which certain HLA types predispose or protect against disease are currently unclear.
source: The molecular mechanisms by which certain HLA types predispose or protect against disease are currently unclear.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this knowledge gap.

claim: The mechanistic underpinnings underlying associations with some autoimmune diseases may be due to certain HLA types being more likely than other HLA types to atypically present self-antigens.
source: Several studies have suggested that the mechanistic underpinnings underlying associations with some autoimmune diseases may be due to certain HLA types being more likely than other HLA types to atypically present self-antigens (Klein et al., 2014; Oldstone, 1998; Yin et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies suggesting this mechanism.

claim: Expression differences between different HLA types of the same HLA gene could contribute to disease associations.
source: Expression differences between different HLA types of the same HLA gene could also contribute to disease associations.
evidence: The introduction proposes this as a potential mechanism.

claim: Some genetic associations with specific HLA types could be due to causal variants on the same haplotype that affect the expression or function of non-HLA genes in the MHC region.
source: Finally, some of the genetic associations with specific HLA types could be due to causal variants on the same haplotype, that affect the expression or function of non-HLA genes in the MHC region (Holoshitz, 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites a study suggesting this mechanism.

claim: HLA-VBSeq was used to estimate HLA types at eight-digit resolution for 30 genes.
source: We used HLA-VBSeq (Nariai et al., 2015) to estimate HLA types at eight-digit resolution for 30 genes [six HLA class I genes (HLA-A, -B, C, -E, -F, -G); eight HLA Class I pseudogenes (HLA-H, -J, -K, -L, -P, -T, -V, -W); twelve HLA class II genes (HLA-DMA, -DMB, -DOA, -DOB, -DPA1, -DPA2, -DPB1, -DPB2, -DQA1, -DQB1, -DRA, -DRB1); and four non-HLA genes (MICA, MICB, TAP1, and TAP2)] in 650 WGS samples (from 419 unique individuals) and identified 526 unique alleles (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The Results section describes the HLA typing method and results.

claim: 526 unique alleles were identified across 30 genes in 650 WGS samples from 419 unique individuals.
source: We used HLA-VBSeq (Nariai et al., 2015) to estimate HLA types at eight-digit resolution for 30 genes [six HLA class I genes (HLA-A, -B, C, -E, -F, -G); eight HLA Class I pseudogenes (HLA-H, -J, -K, -L, -P, -T, -V, -W); twelve HLA class II genes (HLA-DMA, -DMB, -DOA, -DOB, -DPA1, -DPA2, -DPB1, -DPB2, -DQA1, -DQB1, -DRA, -DRB1); and four non-HLA genes (MICA, MICB, TAP1, and TAP2)] in 650 WGS samples (from 419 unique individuals) and identified 526 unique alleles (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The Results section reports the number of unique alleles identified.

claim: The 650 WGS samples were obtained by combining data from iPSCORE (273 individuals) and HipSci (377 samples from 146 individuals).
source: The 650 WGS samples were obtained by combining data from two large induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) resources: 1) iPSCORE (273 individuals) (Panopoulos et al., 2017), and 2) HipSci (377 samples from 146 individuals) (Kilpinen et al., 2017a; Kilpinen et al., 2017b; Streeter et al., 2017).
evidence: The Results section describes the sources of WGS data with citations.

claim: All WGS samples had deep coverage and the expected high polymorphism rate across the MHC region.
source: All the WGS samples had deep coverage and the expected high polymorphism rate across the MHC region (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The Results section states this observation with reference to figures showing coverage and polymorphism data.

claim: The 146 HipSci individuals were of European descent.
source: The 146 individuals in HipSci were of European descent while the 273 iPSCORE individuals are of diverse ethnic backgrounds (190 European, 30 Asian, 20 Multiple ethnicities, 18 Hispanic, 7 African American, 5 Indian and 3 Middle Eastern) and thus harbored HLA alleles from multiple human populations (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The Results section describes the ethnic composition of the HipSci cohort.

claim: The 273 iPSCORE individuals are of diverse ethnic backgrounds including 190 European, 30 Asian, 20 Multiple ethnicities, 18 Hispanic, 7 African American, 5 Indian and 3 Middle Eastern.
source: The 146 individuals in HipSci were of European descent while the 273 iPSCORE individuals are of diverse ethnic backgrounds (190 European, 30 Asian, 20 Multiple ethnicities, 18 Hispanic, 7 African American, 5 Indian and 3 Middle Eastern) and thus harbored HLA alleles from multiple human populations (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The Results section provides the ethnic breakdown of the iPSCORE cohort.

claim: iPSCORE individuals harbored HLA alleles from multiple human populations.
source: The 146 individuals in HipSci were of European descent while the 273 iPSCORE individuals are of diverse ethnic backgrounds (190 European, 30 Asian, 20 Multiple ethnicities, 18 Hispanic, 7 African American, 5 Indian and 3 Middle Eastern) and thus harbored HLA alleles from multiple human populations (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The Results section infers this from the diverse ethnic backgrounds.

claim: All 146 HipSci donors were unrelated.
source: While all 146 HipSci donors were unrelated, there were 183 donors in iPSCORE that are part of 56 unique families (2–14 individuals/family), including 25 monozygotic (MZ) twin pairs.
evidence: The Results section states the relatedness structure of the HipSci cohort.

claim: There were 183 donors in iPSCORE that are part of 56 unique families (2–14 individuals/family), including 25 monozygotic twin pairs.
source: While all 146 HipSci donors were unrelated, there were 183 donors in iPSCORE that are part of 56 unique families (2–14 individuals/family), including 25 monozygotic (MZ) twin pairs.
evidence: The Results section describes the family structure in the iPSCORE cohort.

claim: For 84 HipSci individuals, 231 matched fibroblast-iPSC WGS pairs were HLA typed (one fibroblast sample and two or more iPSC clones per donor).
source: For 84 HipSci individuals, we HLA typed 231 matched fibroblast-iPSC WGS pairs (one fibroblast sample and two or more iPSC clones per donor).
evidence: The Results section describes the paired samples analyzed.

claim: A high recall rate was observed for all 30 genes (mean = 98.5% for both iPSCORE and HipSci samples).
source: We observed a high recall rate for all 30 genes (mean = 98.5% for both iPSCORE and HipSci samples, Figure 2C,D) and for only three HLA genes in iPSCORE (HLA-H, HLA-T and HLA-K) and four genes in HipSci (HLA-H, HLA-T, HLA-K and HLA-DRB1) fewer than 95% of individuals were HLA-typed.
evidence: The Results section reports the recall rates with reference to figures.

claim: For only three HLA genes in iPSCORE (HLA-H, HLA-T and HLA-K) fewer than 95% of individuals were HLA-typed.
source: We observed a high recall rate for all 30 genes (mean = 98.5% for both iPSCORE and HipSci samples, Figure 2C,D) and for only three HLA genes in iPSCORE (HLA-H, HLA-T and HLA-K) and four genes in HipSci (HLA-H, HLA-T, HLA-K and HLA-DRB1) fewer than 95% of individuals were HLA-typed.
evidence: The Results section identifies specific genes with lower recall rates.

claim: For four genes in HipSci (HLA-H, HLA-T, HLA-K and HLA-DRB1) fewer than 95% of individuals were HLA-typed.
source: We observed a high recall rate for all 30 genes (mean = 98.5% for both iPSCORE and HipSci samples, Figure 2C,D) and for only three HLA genes in iPSCORE (HLA-H, HLA-T and HLA-K) and four genes in HipSci (HLA-H, HLA-T, HLA-K and HLA-DRB1) fewer than 95% of individuals were HLA-typed.
evidence: The Results section identifies specific genes with lower recall rates in HipSci.

claim: The fraction of heterozygous and homozygous HLA types across the 30 genes was highly similar in the iPSCORE and HipSci individuals (r = 0.92).
source: The fraction of heterozygous and homozygous HLA types across the 30 genes was highly similar in the iPSCORE and HipSci individuals (r = 0.92).
evidence: The Results section reports the correlation between the two cohorts.

claim: The median concordance across all 526 HLA alleles was very high for twin pairs (96.7%), fibroblast-iPSC pairs (95.7%), and Mendelian inheritance (90.9%).
source: Overall, we found that the median concordance across for all 526 HLA alleles was very high; however, both the twin pairs (96.7%) and fibroblast-iPSC pairs (95.7%) had slightly higher concordance than the Mendelian inheritance (90.9%, Figure 2E,F,G).
evidence: The Results section reports concordance values with reference to figures.

claim: Twin pairs (96.7%) and fibroblast-iPSC pairs (95.7%) had slightly higher concordance than Mendelian inheritance (90.9%).
source: Overall, we found that the median concordance across for all 526 HLA alleles was very high; however, both the twin pairs (96.7%) and fibroblast-iPSC pairs (95.7%) had slightly higher concordance than the Mendelian inheritance (90.9%, Figure 2E,F,G).
evidence: The Results section compares concordance values across different validation approaches.

claim: HLA-VBSeq produces highly reproducible results when samples with exactly the same two HLA alleles are analyzed.
source: These results show that HLA-VBSeq produces highly reproducible results when samples with exactly the same two HLA alleles are analyzed; but has slightly lower reproducibility calling the same HLA alleles when in different diplotypes.
evidence: The Results section interprets the concordance data.

claim: HLA-VBSeq has slightly lower reproducibility calling the same HLA alleles when in different diplotypes.
source: These results show that HLA-VBSeq produces highly reproducible results when samples with exactly the same two HLA alleles are analyzed; but has slightly lower reproducibility calling the same HLA alleles when in different diplotypes.
evidence: The Results section interprets the concordance data to identify a limitation.

claim: The vast majority (511, 97.1%) of HLA alleles were in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (p>1×10−6).
source: To estimate the accuracy of the 526 called HLA alleles we tested for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) in the unrelated individuals and found that the vast majority (511, 97.1%) were in HWE (p>1×10−6, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), consistent with the reproducibility values in twin pairs (96.7%) and in fibroblast-iPSC pairs (95.7%).
evidence: The Results section reports HWE testing results with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The HWE results are consistent with the reproducibility values in twin pairs (96.7%) and in fibroblast-iPSC pairs (95.7%).
source: To estimate the accuracy of the 526 called HLA alleles we tested for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) in the unrelated individuals and found that the vast majority (511, 97.1%) were in HWE (p>1×10−6, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), consistent with the reproducibility values in twin pairs (96.7%) and in fibroblast-iPSC pairs (95.7%).
evidence: The Results section compares HWE results with reproducibility measures.

claim: High correlation was observed between HLA allele frequencies in AFND and iPSCORE (r = 0.921) and HipSci (r = 0.908).
source: We also conducted a comparative analysis with HLA alleles in 3.5 million individuals with diverse genetic backgrounds from the Allele Frequency Net Database (AFND) (González-Galarza et al., 2015) and observed high correlation between HLA allele frequencies in AFND and iPSCORE (r = 0.921) and HipSci (r = 0.908, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The Results section reports correlation with external database with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: HLA-VBSeq was able to accurately detect eight-digit resolution HLA alleles in the 650 WGS samples as evidenced by high recall rates, reproducibility and allele frequencies consistent with Hardy-Weinberg law.
source: Overall, HLA-VBSeq (Nariai et al., 2015) was able to accurately detect eight-digit resolution HLA alleles in the 650 WGS samples as evidenced by high recall rates, reproducibility and allele frequencies consistent with Hardy-Weinberg law.
evidence: The Results section summarizes the validation of HLA typing accuracy.

claim: RNA-seq data from 446 iPSC samples (derived from 361 of the HLA typed individuals) was used to analyze gene expression.
source: To analyze gene expression, we used RNA-seq data from 446 iPSC samples (derived from 361 of the HLA typed individuals Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The Results section describes the RNA-seq data used for expression analysis.

claim: There were 146 expressed genes in the MHC interval (TPM >2 in at least 10 samples).
source: There were 146 expressed genes in the MHC interval (TPM >2 in at least 10 samples), of which 24 were HLA genes, including six HLA class I genes, 3 HLA class I pseudogenes, 11 HLA class II genes, MICA, MICB, TAP1 and TAP2.
evidence: The Results section reports the number of expressed genes with the expression threshold used.

claim: 24 of the 146 expressed genes were HLA genes, including six HLA class I genes, 3 HLA class I pseudogenes, 11 HLA class II genes, MICA, MICB, TAP1 and TAP2.
source: There were 146 expressed genes in the MHC interval (TPM >2 in at least 10 samples), of which 24 were HLA genes, including six HLA class I genes, 3 HLA class I pseudogenes, 11 HLA class II genes, MICA, MICB, TAP1 and TAP2.
evidence: The Results section breaks down the types of HLA genes expressed.

claim: HLA class I genes tended to be expressed at high levels, consistent with their ubiquitous expression in all cell types.
source: The HLA class I genes tended to be expressed at high levels, consistent with their ubiquitous expression in all cell types, and the HLA class II genes tended to be expressed at lower levels, as expected due to their primary role in immune cells (Matzaraki et al., 2017).
evidence: The Results section describes expression patterns with biological interpretation and citation.

claim: HLA class II genes tended to be expressed at lower levels, as expected due to their primary role in immune cells.
source: The HLA class I genes tended to be expressed at high levels, consistent with their ubiquitous expression in all cell types, and the HLA class II genes tended to be expressed at lower levels, as expected due to their primary role in immune cells (Matzaraki et al., 2017).
evidence: The Results section describes expression patterns with biological interpretation and citation.

claim: 189 of 428 HLA types (44.2%) present in at least two individuals showed significantly different expression levels of the cognate HLA gene compared with samples not carrying the HLA type (t-test, FDR < 5%).
source: We observed high variability in the expression levels of the different HLA alleles, with 189 of 428 HLA types (44.2%) present in at least two individuals showing a significantly different expression level of the cognate HLA gene compared with the samples not carrying the HLA type (t-test, FDR < 5%, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The Results section reports the number and percentage of HLA types with differential expression.

claim: Five HLA genes (HLA-A, HLA-C, HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQB1 and HLA-DPB1) showed more than four-fold differences between the least expressed and the most expressed alleles.
source: Five HLA genes (HLA-A, HLA-C, HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQB1 and HLA-DPB1) showed more than four-fold differences between the least expressed and the most expressed alleles.
evidence: The Results section identifies specific genes with large expression differences between alleles.

claim: The class I genes of 8.1AH tended to be expressed higher than the other HLA types of the cognate gene.
source: We examined the HLA types corresponding to the 8.1AH at eight-digit resolution (Figure 1B), and determined that the class I genes tended to be expressed higher than the other HLA types of the cognate gene, while two of the class II genes (HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1) were significantly expressed lower and one (HLA-DRB1) was not differentially expressed (Figure 3C–H).
evidence: The Results section describes expression patterns of 8.1AH alleles with reference to figures.

claim: Two of the class II genes of 8.1AH (HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1) were significantly expressed lower than other HLA types.
source: We examined the HLA types corresponding to the 8.1AH at eight-digit resolution (Figure 1B), and determined that the class I genes tended to be expressed higher than the other HLA types of the cognate gene, while two of the class II genes (HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1) were significantly expressed lower and one (HLA-DRB1) was not differentially expressed (Figure 3C–H).
evidence: The Results section describes expression patterns of 8.1AH alleles with reference to figures.

claim: HLA-DRB1 of 8.1AH was not differentially expressed compared to other HLA types.
source: We examined the HLA types corresponding to the 8.1AH at eight-digit resolution (Figure 1B), and determined that the class I genes tended to be expressed higher than the other HLA types of the cognate gene, while two of the class II genes (HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1) were significantly expressed lower and one (HLA-DRB1) was not differentially expressed (Figure 3C–H).
evidence: The Results section describes expression patterns of 8.1AH alleles with reference to figures.

claim: Eight-digit HLA types were strongly associated with expression differences of the cognate HLA gene.
source: Overall, eight-digit HLA types were strongly associated with expression differences of the cognate HLA gene, suggesting that the associations between HLA types and disease may in part be driven by differential allelic expression.
evidence: The Results section summarizes the association between HLA types and expression.

claim: The associations between HLA types and disease may in part be driven by differential allelic expression.
source: Overall, eight-digit HLA types were strongly associated with expression differences of the cognate HLA gene, suggesting that the associations between HLA types and disease may in part be driven by differential allelic expression.
evidence: The Results section suggests this mechanism based on the expression data.

claim: 56 eGenes were detected with associations to 72,473 eQTLs (Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected p-value<0.1) corresponding to 26,363 distinct variants.
source: We performed an eQTL analysis by testing each of the 146 expressed genes and the genotypes of 45,245 variants (MAF >1%) spanning the MHC region (±1 Mb flanking each side) using a linear mixed model. We detected associations between 56 eGenes and 72,473 eQTLs (Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected p-value<0.1, Supplementary file 6) corresponding to 26,363 distinct variants; hence 36.4% of the variants in the MHC region were associated with the expression of one or more gene.
evidence: The Results section reports the eQTL analysis results.

claim: 36.4% of the variants in the MHC region were associated with the expression of one or more gene.
source: We performed an eQTL analysis by testing each of the 146 expressed genes and the genotypes of 45,245 variants (MAF >1%) spanning the MHC region (±1 Mb flanking each side) using a linear mixed model. We detected associations between 56 eGenes and 72,473 eQTLs (Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected p-value<0.1, Supplementary file 6) corresponding to 26,363 distinct variants; hence 36.4% of the variants in the MHC region were associated with the expression of one or more gene.
evidence: The Results section calculates the percentage of variants with eQTL associations.

claim: The 56 eGenes tended to be associated with high numbers of primary eQTLs (median = 842), ranging from 26 (HLA-E) to 4911 (HLA-DQB1).
source: The 56 eGenes tended to be associated with high numbers of primary eQTLs (median = 842), ranging from 26 (HLA-E) to 4911 (HLA-DQB1).
evidence: The Results section describes the distribution of eQTLs per eGene.

claim: Many eGenes were associated with primary eQTLs spanning relatively large distances (median = 2.1 Mb).
source: Many of the eGenes were also associated with primary eQTLs spanning relatively large distances (median = 2.1 Mb), including ZFP57, HLA-C, HLA-B, MICA and RNF5, whose associated primary eQTLs nearly spanned the entire 4 Mb MHC region, which is consistent with the strong LD of ancestral haplotypes.
evidence: The Results section describes the genomic span of eQTLs.

claim: ZFP57, HLA-C, HLA-B, MICA and RNF5 had associated primary eQTLs that nearly spanned the entire 4 Mb MHC region.
source: Many of the eGenes were also associated with primary eQTLs spanning relatively large distances (median = 2.1 Mb), including ZFP57, HLA-C, HLA-B, MICA and RNF5, whose associated primary eQTLs nearly spanned the entire 4 Mb MHC region, which is consistent with the strong LD of ancestral haplotypes.
evidence: The Results section identifies specific genes with region-wide eQTL associations.

claim: The wide span of eQTLs is consistent with the strong LD of ancestral haplotypes.
source: Many of the eGenes were also associated with primary eQTLs spanning relatively large distances (median = 2.1 Mb), including ZFP57, HLA-C, HLA-B, MICA and RNF5, whose associated primary eQTLs nearly spanned the entire 4 Mb MHC region, which is consistent with the strong LD of ancestral haplotypes.
evidence: The Results section interprets the eQTL span in the context of LD structure.

claim: Gene expression in the MHC is associated with cis regulatory variants that span regions several times larger than those normally tested in genome-wide eQTL analyses.
source: While genome-wide eQTL analyses usually test associations between gene expression and neighboring variants (within 500 kb or 1 Mb), our results show that gene expression in the MHC is associated with cis regulatory variants that span regions several times larger than those normally tested.
evidence: The Results section contrasts MHC eQTL patterns with typical genome-wide patterns.

claim: For 42 eGenes, secondary eQTLs were observed (conditional on the lead eQTL).
source: To identify independent eQTLs, we repeated the analysis conditioning gene expression on the lead eQTL for each of the 56 eGenes. For 42 eGenes, we observed secondary eQTLs (conditional on the lead eQTL), and for 36 eGenes we identified a tertiary eQTL upon conditioning on the top two independent eQTLs (Figure 4, Figure 5).
evidence: The Results section reports conditional eQTL analysis results.

claim: For 36 eGenes, a tertiary eQTL was identified upon conditioning on the top two independent eQTLs.
source: To identify independent eQTLs, we repeated the analysis conditioning gene expression on the lead eQTL for each of the 56 eGenes. For 42 eGenes, we observed secondary eQTLs (conditional on the lead eQTL), and for 36 eGenes we identified a tertiary eQTL upon conditioning on the top two independent eQTLs (Figure 4, Figure 5).
evidence: The Results section reports conditional eQTL analysis results.

claim: For the 56 eGenes, 76,809 eQTLs (72,473 primary, 2424 conditional 1 and 1912 conditional 2, Bonferroni-adjusted p-value<0.1) were observed with genome-wide significance corresponding to 27,200 distinct variants.
source: Overall, for the 56 eGenes, we observed 76,809 eQTLs (72,473 primary, 2424 conditional 1 and 1912 conditional 2, Bonferroni-adjusted p-value<0.1) with genome-wide significance corresponding to 27,200 distinct variants.
evidence: The Results section summarizes the total number of eQTLs identified.

claim: Within the gene-dense MHC region, a large fraction (56; 38.4%) of the expressed genes are eGenes.
source: These results show that, within the gene-dense MHC region, a large fraction (56; 38.4%) of the expressed genes are eGenes, many of which (42; 75%) are associated with multiple independent regulatory variants that span long distances.
evidence: The Results section calculates the percentage of expressed genes that are eGenes.

claim: Many eGenes (42; 75%) are associated with multiple independent regulatory variants that span long distances.
source: These results show that, within the gene-dense MHC region, a large fraction (56; 38.4%) of the expressed genes are eGenes, many of which (42; 75%) are associated with multiple independent regulatory variants that span long distances.
evidence: The Results section calculates the percentage of eGenes with multiple independent eQTLs.

claim: For 13 eGenes (23.2%), the lead eQTL was localized within 5 kb of their TSS.
source: We initially investigated the distance between lead eQTLs and the transcription start site (TSS) of their associated eGene and found that in general they were close (median distance = 18.3 kb, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and for 13 eGenes (23.2%), the lead eQTL was localized within 5 kb of their TSS.
evidence: The Results section reports the proximity of lead eQTLs to TSS.

claim: The median distance between lead eQTLs and the TSS of their associated eGene was 18.3 kb.
source: We initially investigated the distance between lead eQTLs and the transcription start site (TSS) of their associated eGene and found that in general they were close (median distance = 18.3 kb, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and for 13 eGenes (23.2%), the lead eQTL was localized within 5 kb of their TSS.
evidence: The Results section reports the median distance of lead eQTLs from TSS.

claim: eQTLs in the MHC region with the largest effect sizes were enriched for overlapping regulatory elements active in iPSCs including active transcription start sites, regions flanking active TSS, UTRs and transcribed regions.
source: We examined if the 76,809 primary and conditional eQTLs (27,200 distinct variants) were enriched in regulatory elements by testing their overlap with chromatin states in iPSC lines from the Roadmap Epigenomics Consortium (Kundaje et al., 2015). We observed that the eQTLs in the MHC region with the largest effect sizes were enriched for overlapping regulatory elements active in iPSCs including active transcription start sites (TSS), regions flanking active TSS, UTRs (defined as regions transcribed at 5' and 3') and transcribed regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Results section reports enrichment analysis results with citation and reference to supplementary figure.

claim: eGenes were significantly more likely to have allele-specific expression than the other 90 expressed MHC genes (mean allelic imbalance fraction = 67.3% vs 61.9%, p=4.38×10−64, Mann-Whitney U test).
source: To further characterize the associations between eQTLs and gene expression, we tested if the 56 eGenes were more likely to have allele-specific expression (ASE) than the other 90 expressed MHC genes; and found that eGenes were significantly more likely to have ASE [mean allelic imbalance fraction (AIF) = 67.3%, compared with 61.9% in the other genes, p=4.38×10−64, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 7].
evidence: The Results section reports ASE analysis results with statistical test.

claim: eGenes in samples with heterozygous eQTLs (primary and conditional) have stronger ASE compared with eGenes in samples homozygous for eQTLs.
source: We also observed that eGenes in samples with heterozygous eQTLs (primary and conditional) have stronger ASE compared with eGenes in samples homozygous for eQTLs (39,891 eQTLs in total examined, corresponding to 21,739 variants; Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The Results section reports ASE differences based on eQTL genotype.

claim: The primary and conditional eQTLs in the HLA region have characteristics of regulatory variants including proximity to the TSS of their associated eGene, enrichment in active chromatin marks, and association with allele-specific expression of their eGene.
source: These results show that the primary and conditional eQTLs in the HLA region have characteristics of regulatory variants including proximity to the TSS of their associated eGene, enrichment in active chromatin marks, and association with allele-specific expression of their eGene.
evidence: The Results section summarizes the validation of eQTLs as regulatory variants.

claim: 1480 loci with posterior probability of association (PPA) >0.2 for sharing the same causal variant were identified between eQTL signals and GWAS signals for 4083 complex traits.
source: We tested the eQTL signals (primary and conditional) for all 56 MHC eGenes against the GWAS signals for 4083 complex traits from the UK Biobank and as expected identified many strong associations (1480 loci with posterior probability of association (PPA) >0.2 for sharing the same causal variant, including 180 with PPA >0.8, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: The Results section reports colocalization analysis results.

claim: 180 loci with PPA >0.8 for sharing the same causal variant were identified between eQTL signals and GWAS signals.
source: We tested the eQTL signals (primary and conditional) for all 56 MHC eGenes against the GWAS signals for 4083 complex traits from the UK Biobank and as expected identified many strong associations (1480 loci with posterior probability of association (PPA) >0.2 for sharing the same causal variant, including 180 with PPA >0.8, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: The Results section reports high-confidence colocalization results.

claim: Eight eGenes were identified whose eQTL colocalized with GWAS signals for pulmonary diseases.
source: We identified eight eGenes whose eQTL colocalized with GWAS signals for pulmonary diseases, of which three, HLA-B, HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1, had been previously associated with Asthma in GWAS (Kontakioti et al., 2014; Li et al., 2012; Mahdi et al., 2018) and in the UK Biobank (Vicente et al., 2017).
evidence: The Results section reports colocalization with pulmonary disease GWAS.

claim: Three eGenes (HLA-B, HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1) had been previously associated with Asthma in GWAS and in the UK Biobank.
source: We identified eight eGenes whose eQTL colocalized with GWAS signals for pulmonary diseases, of which three, HLA-B, HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1, had been previously associated with Asthma in GWAS (Kontakioti et al., 2014; Li et al., 2012; Mahdi et al., 2018) and in the UK Biobank (Vicente et al., 2017).
evidence: The Results section cites previous GWAS findings for these genes.

claim: Five novel eGenes (HLA-DRA, APOM, DXO, RNF5 and TAP1) associated with pulmonary diseases were identified that had not been identified in GWAS.
source: However, the other five eGenes, including HLA-DRA (the most strongly associated), APOM, DXO, RNF5 and TAP1 were novel, that is had not been identified in GWAS.
evidence: The Results section identifies novel associations not previously found in GWAS.

claim: The association of RNF5 with pulmonary diseases is consistent with its function as a regulator of the CFTR protein and suggested role in cystic fibrosis.
source: Interestingly, the association of RNF5 was consistent with its function as a regulator of the CFTR protein and suggested role in cystic fibrosis (Sondo et al., 2018; Tomati et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section interprets the RNF5 association in the context of known biology with citations.

claim: Four novel eGenes (EHMT2, GPANK1, HLA-C and RNF5) were identified as associated with weight phenotypes.
source: We next identified four novel eGenes (EHMT2, GPANK1, HLA-C and RNF5) associated with weight phenotypes.
evidence: The Results section identifies novel associations with weight phenotypes.

claim: GPANK1 was only associated with fat-free mass, suggesting that the protein product is involved in muscle or bone mass regulation.
source: The two eGenes most strongly associated, GPANK1 and RNF5, had opposite associations. GPANK1 was only associated with fat-free mass, suggesting that the protein product is involved in muscle or bone mass regulation.
evidence: The Results section interprets the GPANK1 association pattern.

claim: RNF5 was more strongly associated with fat mass than fat-free mass.
source: Conversely, RNF5 was more strongly associated with fat mass than fat-free mass, suggesting that its altered expression can contribute to CF phenotypic variation, as these individuals are known to have bile and other digestive issues, including difficulties in assimilating fat (Bijvelds et al., 2005; Freudenberg et al., 2008; Morison et al., 1997; Wilke et al., 2011).
evidence: The Results section describes the RNF5 association pattern with weight phenotypes.

claim: Altered RNF5 expression can contribute to CF phenotypic variation, as CF individuals are known to have bile and other digestive issues, including difficulties in assimilating fat.
source: Conversely, RNF5 was more strongly associated with fat mass than fat-free mass, suggesting that its altered expression can contribute to CF phenotypic variation, as these individuals are known to have bile and other digestive issues, including difficulties in assimilating fat (Bijvelds et al., 2005; Freudenberg et al., 2008; Morison et al., 1997; Wilke et al., 2011).
evidence: The Results section interprets the RNF5 association in the context of CF pathophysiology with citations.

claim: eQTLs for HLA-DQB1, PSORS1C2 and RNF5 colocalized with liver and gallbladder GWAS signals.
source: Finally, eQTLs for HLA-DQB1, PSORS1C2 and RNF5 colocalized with liver and gallbladder GWAS signals.
evidence: The Results section reports colocalization with liver and gallbladder disease GWAS.

claim: Altered gene expression levels in the MHC region are associated with phenotypic variation in CF patients.
source: These findings suggest that altered gene expression levels in the MHC region are associated with phenotypic variation in CF patients.
evidence: The Results section interprets the colocalization findings in the context of CF.

claim: 1139 associations were detected between 250 HLA-type eQTLs and 114 eGenes.
source: We detected 1139 associations between 250 HLA-type eQTLs and 114 eGenes (Supplementary file 9, Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The Results section reports HLA-type eQTL analysis results.

claim: Associations between HLA-type eQTLs and gene expression primarily occurred between HLA-type eQTLs and genes located in their proximity (median distance = 146.2 kb for significant associations compared with 1.35 Mb for non-significant associations, p=2.7×10−67, Mann-Whitney U test).
source: Associations primarily occurred between HLA-type eQTLs and the expression of genes located in their proximity (median distance = 146.2 kb for significant associations compared with 1.35 Mb for non-significant associations, p=2.7×10−67, Mann-Whitney U test), resulting in HLA-type eQTLs largely clustering into four distinct genomic regions.
evidence: The Results section reports the distance distribution of HLA-type eQTL associations with statistical test.

claim: HLA-type eQTLs largely clustered into four distinct genomic regions.
source: Associations primarily occurred between HLA-type eQTLs and the expression of genes located in their proximity (median distance = 146.2 kb for significant associations compared with 1.35 Mb for non-significant associations, p=2.7×10−67, Mann-Whitney U test), resulting in HLA-type eQTLs largely clustering into four distinct genomic regions.
evidence: The Results section describes the spatial clustering of HLA-type eQTLs.

claim: RNF5 showed strong associations with multiple HLA types in clusters 1, 2 and 3.
source: Interestingly, RNF5 showed strong associations with multiple HLA types in clusters 1, 2 and 3, confirming the observation that it had long-range associations with eQTLs spanning the entire MHC region (Figure 4).
evidence: The Results section describes RNF5's unique association pattern.

claim: There were 62 eGenes identified only by the HLA-type eQTL analysis, four identified only by the single-variant eQTL analysis and 52 identified by both analyses.
source: In total, there were 62 eGenes identified only by the HLA-type eQTL analysis, four identified only by the single-variant eQTL analysis and 52 identified by both analyses (44.4% all 118 eGenes; Supplementary file 10).
evidence: The Results section compares the discovery power of the two eQTL approaches.

claim: The HLA-type eQTL analysis had substantially greater power to identify eGenes than the single-variant eQTL analysis.
source: These results show that the HLA-type eQTL analysis had substantially greater power to identify eGenes than the single-variant eQTL analysis.
evidence: The Results section concludes about the relative power of the two approaches.

claim: The number of HLA-type eQTLs was highly correlated with the number of eQTLs (r = 0.829, p=7.9×10−31).
source: We observed that the number of HLA-type eQTLs was highly correlated with the number of eQTLs (r = 0.829, p=7.9×10−31, Figure 5C).
evidence: The Results section reports the correlation between the two types of eQTL counts.

claim: 406 HLA-type eQTLs conditional on the lead eQTLs (49 eGenes) were observed.
source: We observed 406 HLA-type eQTLs conditional on the lead eQTLs (49 eGenes), 316 HLA-type eQTLs conditional on the top two independent eQTLs (27 eGenes) and 150 HLA-type eQTLs (13 eGenes) conditional on the top three independent eQTLs (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The Results section reports conditional HLA-type eQTL analysis results.

claim: 316 HLA-type eQTLs conditional on the top two independent eQTLs (27 eGenes) were observed.
source: We observed 406 HLA-type eQTLs conditional on the lead eQTLs (49 eGenes), 316 HLA-type eQTLs conditional on the top two independent eQTLs (27 eGenes) and 150 HLA-type eQTLs (13 eGenes) conditional on the top three independent eQTLs (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The Results section reports conditional HLA-type eQTL analysis results.

claim: 150 HLA-type eQTLs (13 eGenes) conditional on the top three independent eQTLs were observed.
source: We observed 406 HLA-type eQTLs conditional on the lead eQTLs (49 eGenes), 316 HLA-type eQTLs conditional on the top two independent eQTLs (27 eGenes) and 150 HLA-type eQTLs (13 eGenes) conditional on the top three independent eQTLs (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The Results section reports conditional HLA-type eQTL analysis results.

claim: The conditional HLA-eQTLs were largely confined to the four genomic regions containing clusters of genes with shared HLA-eQTLs and the RNF5 gene.
source: Of note, the conditional HLA-eQTLs were largely confined to the four genomic regions containing clusters of genes with shared HLA-eQTLs and the RNF5 gene.
evidence: The Results section describes the spatial distribution of conditional HLA-type eQTLs.

claim: The HLA-eQTL analysis identifies a different set of regulatory variants than the single-variant eQTL analysis even for the 52 eGenes discovered by both analyses.
source: These findings show that the HLA-eQTL analysis identifies a different set of regulatory variants than the single-variant eQTL analysis even for the 52 eGenes discovered by both analyses.
evidence: The Results section concludes about the complementary nature of the two approaches.

claim: Different eGenes in each cluster were typically associated with the genotypes of different HLA types, suggesting that the observed clustering was not due to co-expression of neighboring HLA genes.
source: We observed that different eGenes in each cluster were typically associated with the genotypes of different HLA types, suggesting that the observed clustering was not due to co-expression (i.e., correlated expression levels) of neighboring HLA genes (Figure 7).
evidence: The Results section interprets the clustering pattern with reference to figure.

claim: The expression of both HLA-DRB5 and HLA-DRB1 was associated with many of the same HLA types.
source: There was one exception in cluster 3, with the expression of both HLA-DRB5 and HLA-DRB1 associated with many of the same HLA types (Figure 7C).
evidence: The Results section identifies an exception to the general pattern.

claim: Only five eGenes in cluster 3 (HLA-DRA, HLA-DRB5, HLA-DQA1, HLA-DQB1 and HLA-DRB1) displayed moderate correlated expression.
source: Only five eGenes in cluster 3 (HLA-DRA, HLA-DRB5, HLA-DQA1, HLA-DQB1 and HLA-DRB1) displayed moderate correlated expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), despite having their expression levels largely associated with different HLA types of neighboring genes (Figure 7).
evidence: The Results section reports co-expression analysis results with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The HLA-type eQTLs capture regulatory variants associated with the expression of one or a few neighboring genes.
source: These findings suggest that the HLA-type eQTLs capture regulatory variants associated with the expression of one or a few neighboring genes.
evidence: The Results section interprets the clustering and co-expression patterns.

claim: Unlike the eQTLs from the single-variant analysis that tend to span long distances most likely due to the strong LD in the MHC region, the HLA-type eQTLs capture regulatory variants that act over relatively short distances.
source: Furthermore, unlike the eQTLs from the single-variant analysis that tend to span long distances most likely due to the strong LD in the MHC region (Figure 4), the HLA-type eQTLs capture regulatory variants that act over relatively short distances.
evidence: The Results section contrasts the spatial patterns of the two types of eQTLs.

claim: The expression of RNF5 was negatively associated with eight-digit HLA types for all six genes composing the 8.1AH.
source: The expression of RNF5 was negatively associated with eight-digit HLA types for all six genes composing the 8.1AH (Figure 8A–F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The Results section reports the association between RNF5 expression and 8.1AH HLA types.

claim: Only one eight-digit HLA type for each of the six genes composing 8.1AH was associated with RNF5 expression.
source: While we discovered several eight-digit resolution HLA types for some of the HLA genes composing 8.1AH (Figure 1), only one eight-digit HLA type for each of the six genes was associated with RNF5 expression.
evidence: The Results section describes the specificity of the RNF5-8.1AH association.

claim: It has been previously proposed that the association between 8.1AH and delayed bacterial colonization in CF patients could be due to the impact of the ancestral HLA-types on the microbiota composition in the lungs.
source: It has been previously proposed that the association between 8.1AH and delayed bacterial colonization in CF patients could be due to the impact of the ancestral HLA-types on the microbiota composition in the lungs (Laki et al., 2006).
evidence: The Results section cites a previous hypothesis about the 8.1AH-CF association.

claim: RNF5 is a current drug target in CF patients because its downregulation contributes to stabilizing and rescuing the function of mutant CFTR proteins.
source: However, our findings, combined with the fact that RNF5 is a current drug target in CF patients because its downregulation contributes to stabilizing and rescuing the function of mutant CFTR proteins (Sondo et al., 2018; Tomati et al., 2015), suggests that the association between 8.1AH CF carriers and delayed bacterial colonization could be due to decreased expression of RNF5 (Lyczak et al., 2002; Mall and Hartl, 2014; McNicholas, 2017; Pier et al., 1996).
evidence: The Results section cites studies showing RNF5 as a drug target in CF.

claim: The association between 8.1AH CF carriers and delayed bacterial colonization could be due to decreased expression of RNF5.
source: However, our findings, combined with the fact that RNF5 is a current drug target in CF patients because its downregulation contributes to stabilizing and rescuing the function of mutant CFTR proteins (Sondo et al., 2018; Tomati et al., 2015), suggests that the association between 8.1AH CF carriers and delayed bacterial colonization could be due to decreased expression of RNF5 (Lyczak et al., 2002; Mall and Hartl, 2014; McNicholas, 2017; Pier et al., 1996).
evidence: The Results section proposes this mechanism based on the study findings and previous literature.

claim: In the proposed model, CF patients carrying 8.1AH express RNF5 at lower levels than non-carriers, resulting in lower protein levels of RNF5 and thereby less degradation of the misfolded mutated CFTR protein, improved Cl- secretion, lower mucus secretion and delayed colonization by S. aureus and P. aeruginosa.
source: In this proposed model, CF patients carrying 8.1AH express RNF5 at lower levels than non-carriers, resulting in lower protein levels of RNF5 and thereby less degradation of the misfolded mutated CFTR protein, improved Cl- secretion, lower mucus secretion and delayed colonization by S. aureus and P. aeruginosa (Figure 8F).
evidence: The Results section describes the proposed mechanistic model with reference to figure.

claim: The MHC region is typically excluded from eQTL studies due to its high SNP frequency and complex LD structure.
source: Although the human MHC region on 6p21.3 has been associated with many autoimmune and infectious diseases, it is typically excluded from eQTL studies due to its high SNP frequency and complex LD structure (Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: The Discussion section cites a study explaining why the MHC region is often excluded from eQTL studies.

claim: iPSCs are well-powered for eQTL mapping.
source: We have previously shown that iPSCs are well-powered for eQTL mapping (Bonder et al., 2019; Jakubosky et al., 2019a; Jakubosky et al., 2019b), have a distinct regulatory landscape relative to somatic tissues (DeBoever et al., 2017), and thereby provide insights into regulatory variants that exert their effects during early development.
evidence: The Discussion section cites previous studies showing iPSCs are suitable for eQTL mapping.

claim: iPSCs have a distinct regulatory landscape relative to somatic tissues.
source: We have previously shown that iPSCs are well-powered for eQTL mapping (Bonder et al., 2019; Jakubosky et al., 2019a; Jakubosky et al., 2019b), have a distinct regulatory landscape relative to somatic tissues (DeBoever et al., 2017), and thereby provide insights into regulatory variants that exert their effects during early development.
evidence: The Discussion section cites a study showing iPSCs have unique regulatory features.

claim: iPSCs provide insights into regulatory variants that exert their effects during early development.
source: We have previously shown that iPSCs are well-powered for eQTL mapping (Bonder et al., 2019; Jakubosky et al., 2019a; Jakubosky et al., 2019b), have a distinct regulatory landscape relative to somatic tissues (DeBoever et al., 2017), and thereby provide insights into regulatory variants that exert their effects during early development.
evidence: The Discussion section infers this advantage of using iPSCs based on their developmental stage.

claim: Future studies using eQTLs from other cell types could increase the number of complex trait loci in the interval that are functionally annotated.
source: While we demonstrate the feasibility of generating a map of regulatory variation for the MHC region and its utility for examining molecular mechanisms underlying disease associations in the interval, future studies using eQTLs from other cell types could increase the number of complex trait loci in the interval that are functionally annotated.
evidence: The Discussion section suggests future directions for expanding the findings.

claim: The associations between certain HLA types and disease may not only be driven by polymorphic amino acid epitopes resulting in differential binding affinities to specific peptides, but also in part by different expression levels.
source: This finding suggests that the associations between certain HLA types and disease may not only be driven by polymorphic amino acid epitopes resulting in differential binding affinities to specific peptides, but also in part by different expression levels.
evidence: The Discussion section interprets the expression findings in the context of disease mechanisms.

claim: The 8.1 ancestral haplotype (8.1AH) is an important genetic modifier of lung disease in Cystic Fibrosis (CF) patients.
source: Given that the 8.1 ancestral haplotype (8.1AH) is an important genetic modifier of lung disease in Cystic Fibrosis (CF) patients (Laki et al., 2006), we examined if any of the MHC eGenes colocalize with loci for complex traits contributing to phenotypic variation in CF, including pulmonary diseases (Stoltz et al., 2015), weight (Leung et al., 2017; Morison et al., 1997), as well as liver, biliary tract and gallbladder diseases (Assis and Debray, 2017; Diwakar et al., 2001; Herrmann et al., 2010).
evidence: The Discussion section cites a study showing 8.1AH modifies CF lung disease.

claim: Future GWAS directly testing associations between HLA types and complex traits are likely to uncover many novel associations.
source: Based on our findings, future GWAS directly testing associations between HLA types and complex traits are likely to uncover many novel associations.
evidence: The Discussion section predicts future findings based on the current study results.

claim: RNF5 was recently described as a potential novel drug target in CF, because when RNF5 activity is decreased, the mutant CFTR protein becomes stabilized and its function as a cAMP-dependent chloride channel in the lung epithelium is partially rescued.
source: We showed that RNF5 expression was negatively associated with eight-digit HLA types for all six genes composing the 8.1AH. Interestingly, RNF5 was recently described as a potential novel drug target in CF, because, when RNF5 activity is decreased, the mutant CFTR protein becomes stabilized and its function as a cAMP-dependent chloride channel in the lung epithelium is partially rescued (Sondo et al., 2018; Tomati et al., 2015).
evidence: The Discussion section cites studies describing RNF5 as a drug target in CF.

claim: Impaired ion transport mediated by CFTR is associated with reduced airway hydration and decreased mucociliary clearance, which leads to increased vulnerability to bacterial infection.
source: Impaired ion transport mediated by CFTR is associated with reduced airway hydration and decreased mucociliary clearance, which leads to increased vulnerability to bacterial infection (Dechecchi et al., 2018; Munder and Tümmler, 2015).
evidence: The Discussion section cites studies describing the pathophysiology of CF.

claim: Downregulation of RNF5 expression due to the presence of specific regulatory variants in 8.1AH is the likely mechanism underlying delayed colonization by S. aureus and P. aeruginosa.
source: Hence, we postulate that downregulation of RNF5 expression due to the presence of specific regulatory variants in 8.1AH is the likely mechanism underlying delayed colonization by S. aureus and P. aeruginosa.
evidence: The Discussion section postulates this mechanism based on the study findings and previous literature.

claim: The findings do not preclude that HLA types comprising 8.1AH have a direct role in the protection against bacterial colonization in CF.
source: While our findings do not preclude that HLA types comprising 8.1AH have a direct role in the protection against bacterial colonization in CF, they suggest that reduced RNF5 expression likely plays a major factor in the association between 8.1AH and colonization.
evidence: The Discussion section acknowledges alternative mechanisms while emphasizing the RNF5 mechanism.

claim: Reduced RNF5 expression likely plays a major factor in the association between 8.1AH and colonization.
source: While our findings do not preclude that HLA types comprising 8.1AH have a direct role in the protection against bacterial colonization in CF, they suggest that reduced RNF5 expression likely plays a major factor in the association between 8.1AH and colonization.
evidence: The Discussion section emphasizes the importance of RNF5 expression in the 8.1AH-CF association.

claim: Disease associations with HLA types cannot only be due to epitope differences but differential expression of HLA genes and associated non-HLA genes.
source: Taken together, our data provide insights into the genetic architecture of the MHC region and show that disease associations with HLA types cannot only be due to epitope differences but differential expression of HLA genes and associated non-HLA genes.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes the main conclusion about disease mechanisms.

claim: The data are a valuable resource for both the genetics and disease-focus communities that can be exploited to identify causal mechanisms underlying disease associations in the MHC region, and potentially novel drug targets.
source: Further, these data are a valuable resource for both the genetics and disease-focus communities that can be exploited to identify causal mechanisms underlying disease associations in the MHC region, and potentially novel drug targets.
evidence: The Discussion section emphasizes the utility of the resource for future research.
